entry.title: Stop Using .any? the Wrong Way in Rails
entry.summary:
A single block passed to .any? can silently load thousands of records into memory. No warnings. No errors. Just unnecessary objects. And most Rails developers don’t notice it. You’ve probably used both .any? and .exists? in your Rails app without thinking twice. They both answer the same simple question: Is there at least one record? But under the hood, they can behave very differently. In this article, we’ll look at what actually happens when you call each method, when to use which, and how to avoid a common performance trap. If you just need to check whether a relation contains any records at all, both .any? and .exists? generate the same efficient query. user.posts.any? # SELECT 1 AS one FROM "posts" WHERE "posts"."user_id" = 1 LIMIT 1
